en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Three Hundred Lines, titled "The Diamond-Cutter."
Homage to the Blessed Noble Perfection of Wisdom.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great community of twelve hundred monks and with many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī for alms.

Having walked for alms through the great city of Śrāvastī, the Blessed One finished his meal; having returned from his alms-round after the meal, he put away his bowl and robe, washed his feet, and sat down on the seat prepared for him, crossing his legs in the full lotus posture.
Having set his body straight and established mindfulness before him, a great number of monks then approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, and sat down to one side. (1)
Now at that time, the venerable Subhūti was present and seated in that very assembly.

Then the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "It is marvelous, Blessed One!"
It is most wonderful, Sugata, how the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has sustained the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, with the supreme favor.
It is marvelous, Blessed One, how the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has entrusted the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, with the supreme entrustment.

"In that case, Blessed One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle abide, how should they practice, and how should they restrain their mind?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
It is just so, Subhūti."
It is even so, just as you say.
The Tathāgata has sustained the bodhisattva mahāsattvas with the supreme sustenance; the Tathāgata has entrusted the bodhisattva mahāsattvas with the supreme entrustment.

Therefore, Subhūti, listen and attend well and thoroughly; I shall speak to you as to how one who has set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle should stand, how they should practice, and how they should restrain the mind.
"So be it, Blessed One," the Venerable Subhūti replied to the Blessed One. //2//
The Blessed One said this to him: "In this regard, Subhūti, one who has set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle should generate the thought as follows:

'Subhūti, however many beings there are included within the category of beings in the realm of beings—whether born from eggs, or born from a womb, or born from moisture, or born spontaneously; whether possessing form or formless; whether percipient, or non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient.'"
"Whatever extent of the realm of sentient beings is designated when being designated,
all of them must be led by me to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Even though immeasurable sentient beings have been thus led to final nirvana, not a single sentient being has been led to final nirvana."
For what reason?
Subhūti, if the notion of a "being" were to arise in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a "bodhisattva."

For what reason? Subhūti, he for whom the notion of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*) arises, or the notion of a living soul (*jīva-saṃjñā*), or the notion of a person (*pudgala-saṃjñā*) arises, should not be called a bodhisattva. // 3 //
Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not give a gift while dwelling upon a thing;
he should not give a gift while dwelling anywhere;
he should not give a gift while dwelling upon form.
One should not give a gift while remaining fixed upon sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give a gift, such that he does not remain fixed even upon the perception of signs.
Why is that?
Subhūti, for that bodhisattva who gives a gift without abiding, it is not easy to grasp the measure of his mass of merit.
What do you think, Subhūti, is it easy to grasp the measure of space in the eastern direction?
Subhūti said, “Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, “In the same way, is it easy to grasp the measure of space in the south, west, north, below, above, in the intermediate directions, and all around in the ten directions?
Subhūti said, “Certainly not, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said: "It is just so, Subhūti. For a bodhisattva who gives a gift without being established [in anything], Subhūti, it is not easy to grasp the measure of that mass of merit.
In this way, Subhūti, one who has set out on the bodhisattva vehicle should give a gift such that they do not become established even in the perception of signs."
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Tathāgata to be perceived by means of the perfection of his physical marks?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Tathāgata is not to be perceived by means of the perfection of his physical marks."
For what reason?
Blessed One, that perfection of marks which was spoken of by the Tathāgata is itself a non-perfection of marks.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, to whatever extent there is a perfection of marks, to that extent it is false."
As long as there is no perfection of characteristics, so long is it not false; for the Tathāgata is to be seen by way of both characteristics and non-characteristics. // 5 //
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Is it the case, Blessed One,
that there will be some beings in the future time, in the final period, in the final age, during the last five hundred years when the true Dharma is being destroyed,
who will produce the perception of reality when these very words of the sūtras are being spoken?"

Moreover, Subhūti, in the future time, in the final age, in the final period, during the last five hundred years when the true Dharma is in decline, there will indeed be bodhisattva mahāsattvas who will be endowed with virtues, endowed with ethical discipline, and endowed with wisdom.
Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who will produce the perception of reality when such words of the sūtras are being spoken have certainly not attended upon a single buddha,
nor have they planted roots of merit under a single buddha.

Moreover, Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who, when these words of such sūtras are being spoken, shall attain even a single thought of serene faith, will have attended upon many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and will have planted roots of merit under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
Subhūti, they are known by the Tathāgata through his Buddha-knowledge.
Subhūti, those people have been seen by the Tathāgata with his Buddha-eye;
Subhūti, they have been known by the Tathāgata.
Subhūti, all of them will produce and receive an immeasurable and incalculable mass of merit.
For what reason? Because,
Subhūti, the notion of a self does not arise in those bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
nor does the notion of a sentient being.
Neither the notion of a living being nor the notion of a person occurs;
furthermore, Subhūti, the notion of a phenomenon does not occur for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
In this way, there is no perception of non-dharma;
nor, Subhūti, does any perception or non-perception arise in them.
Why is that?
Subhūti, if the notion of a phenomenon (dharma-saṃjñā) were to arise in those bodhisattva mahāsattvas,

that itself would constitute for them a grasping at a self (ātma-grāha), a grasping at a sentient being (sattva-grāha), a grasping at a living soul (jīva-grāha), and a grasping at a person (pudgala-grāha).
If the perception of non-dharma were to arise,
that itself would constitute for them the grasping at a self and the grasping at a sentient being.
"Grasping at a living being, grasping at a person"—
for what reason?
Indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not grasp at a dharma, nor should he grasp at a non-dharma.

Therefore, it was with this intention that the Tathāgata spoke these words: "By those who understand the discourse on the Dharma as being like a raft, even the dharmas themselves must be abandoned, let alone what is not dharma."
Furthermore, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "What do you think, Subhūti,
is there any dharma whatsoever which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as 'unexcelled perfect enlightenment,' or is there any dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata?"
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, O Blessed One,
there is no dharma whatsoever that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as 'unexcelled perfect enlightenment,' nor is there any dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata."
For what reason? That Dharma which has been fully awakened to or taught by the Tathāgata is ungraspable and inexpressible.
That is neither dharma nor adharma. For what reason?
Because noble persons are characterized by the unconditioned. // 7 //

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to fill this great trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce a great mass of merit on that account?"
Subhūti said: "Much, Blessed One;
much, Sugata, would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce from that cause a mass of merit.
Why is that?"
O Blessed One, that heap of merit which was spoken of by the Tathāgata was spoken of by the Tathāgata as no-heap;
therefore the Tathāgata says, "a heap of merit, a heap of merit."

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
and if another were to take up even a single four-line verse from this Dharma-discourse and teach and elucidate it in detail to others—[the latter would generate greater merit]."
This person alone would, on that account, produce a much greater mass of merit, immeasurable and incalculable.
Why is that?
Subhūti, it is because the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is born from this.
And from this have the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, emerged.
Why is that?
Subhūti, as for these so-called "Buddha-dharmas," they have been described by the Tathāgata as indeed no-Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, they are called the Buddha-dharmas. // 8 //
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does it occur to a stream-enterer, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
It does not occur to a stream-enterer, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry.'"
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, he has not entered into any dharma;
therefore he is called a "stream-enterer."
He has not entered into form, nor into sounds, nor into odors, nor into tastes, nor into tangibles, nor into mental phenomena;
therefore he is called a "stream-enterer.
Blessed One, if it should occur to a stream-enterer, "I have attained the fruit of stream-entry," [he would no longer be a stream-enterer].
That itself would be his grasping at a self, grasping at a sentient being, grasping at a living soul, and grasping at a person.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Does it occur to a once-returner, 'I have attained the fruit of a once-returner'?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
It does not occur to that once-returner, 'By me [the fruit of a once-returner has been attained].'"
"The fruit of once-returning has been attained.
For what reason?
Because there is no dharma whatsoever that has attained the state of being a once-returner.
Therefore, he is called a "once-returner."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Does it occur to a non-returner (anāgāmin) that 'I have attained the fruit of non-returning'?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
It does not occur to a non-returner that 'I have attained the fruit of non-returning.'"
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that has attained the state of a non-returner;
therefore it is called "a non-returner."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Does it occur to an Arhat, 'I have attained Arhatship'?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
It does not occur to an Arhat, 'I have attained Arhatship'."
For what reason? Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that is called "Arhat.
It is for this reason that he is called "Arhat."

If, Blessed One, it should occur to an Arhat, "Arhatship has been attained by me," then that itself would be for him a grasping at a self, a grasping at a sentient being, a grasping at a soul, and a grasping at a person.
For what reason?
Blessed One, I have been designated by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, as the foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*).
Blessed One, I am an Arhat, free from passion.
And it did not occur to me, Blessed One, "I am an Arhat, free from passion.

If it had occurred to me, Blessed One, "I have attained Arhatship," the Tathāgata would not have prophesied of me: "The son of good family Subhūti, who dwells in non-contention, is the foremost of those who dwell in non-contention; he does not dwell anywhere."
Therefore, he is called "one who dwells in the state of non-conflict, one who dwells in the state of non-conflict. // 9 //

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti—is there any dharma whatsoever that was received by the Tathāgata from the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
There is no dharma whatsoever that was received by the Tathāgata from the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha."
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva were to say, 'I shall bring about the array of the buddha-field,' he would speak falsely.
Why is that?"
"Subhūti, as for these so-called 'arrays of a buddha-field,' they have been described by the Tathāgata as non-arrays;
therefore they are called 'arrays of a buddha-field.
For that reason, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should produce a mind that is thus non-abiding—a mind that should be produced as not abiding anywhere."
One should not give rise to a mind that is established in form; one should not give rise to a mind that is established in sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
Subhūti, it is as if there were a man possessed of a body, a great body, such that his physical selfhood would be like Sumeru, the king of mountains.
What do you think, Subhūti? Would that physical selfhood be great?
Subhūti said: "That body, Blessed One, would be great; that self-existence, Sugata, would be great. For what reason?"

"O Blessed One, that which is called 'personal existence' (ātmabhāva) is not an existent thing as described by the Tathāgata; therefore it is called 'personal existence. For, O Blessed One, it is neither an existent thing nor a non-existent thing."
Therefore, it is called the personal existence (ātmabhāva). // 10 //
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? If there were as many rivers Ganges as there are grains of sand in the great river Ganges, would the grains of sand in those [rivers] be many?"
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, those Gaṅgā rivers alone would already be many;
how much more so the grains of sand in those Gaṅgā rivers!
The Blessed One said: (Vajr, Vaidya 79)
I declare this to you, Subhūti;

I make it known to you: suppose there were as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in those rivers Ganges, and some woman or man were to fill them with the seven precious jewels and offer them to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats...
"Suppose one were to give a gift to the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
What do you think, Subhūti, would that woman or man produce a great mass of merit on that account?
Subhūti replied, "A great deal, Blessed One."
"O Sugata, would a woman or a man generate a great mass of merit—immeasurable and incalculable—on that account?

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Subhūti, if a woman or a man were to fill as many world-systems as there are with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones,"

And if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having taken up even a single four-line verse from this Dharma-discourse, should teach and proclaim it to others, he or she would thereby produce a much greater mass of merit—immeasurable and incalculable. // 11 //
Moreover, Subhūti, whatever spot of earth this Dharma-discourse is taken up from— even if only a single four-line stanza is recited or proclaimed there—
that spot of earth will become a true shrine for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras; how much more so for those who shall uphold, recite, and master this Dharma-discourse in its entirety?

And they will proclaim it in detail to others. Subhūti, they will be endowed with a supreme wonder. And, Subhūti, on that spot of earth, either the Teacher dwells, or some other person who stands in the place of a wise teacher. // 12 //
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse, and how should I remember it?
When this had been said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, this Dharma-discourse is named 'The Perfection of Wisdom'."
And you should hold it thus.
Why is that?
Subhūti, that very perfection of wisdom which has been taught by the Tathāgata—
That very non-perfection has been spoken of by the Tathāgata;
therefore it is called the perfection of wisdom.
"What do you think, Subhūti—is there any dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
There is no dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is the dust of the earth in a trichiliocosm great in amount?
Subhūti replied: "It is great, Blessed One."
"O Sugata, there would be much dust of the earth.
Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, that which was spoken of by the Tathāgata as the dust of the earth—"
"That which was spoken of by the Blessed One, O Blessed One, as the dust of the earth is not dust; therefore it is called 'the dust of the earth.
And that world-system which was spoken of by the Tathāgata,"
That which was spoken of by the Tathāgata as a "world-system" is, in fact, a non-system;
therefore it is called a "world-system."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, to be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. A Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha is not to be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man."
It should be seen.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, those thirty-two marks of a great man which were spoken of by the Tathāgata—
"Those, Blessed One, have been described by the Tathāgata as being without marks;
therefore they are called the thirty-two marks of a great man."

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Subhūti, if a woman or a man were to sacrifice their own bodies day after day, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and were to continue sacrificing those bodies for as many eons as there are sands in the river Gaṅgā; and if someone else, having taken up even a single four-line stanza from this Dharma-discourse, were to teach and elucidate it to others—"
On that account alone, this person would produce a much greater mass of merit—immeasurable and incalculable. // 13 //
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti shed tears through the force of the Dharma.
Wiping away his tears, he said this to the Blessed One: "It is marvelous, Blessed One;
it is most marvelous, Sugata!"

Since this Dharma discourse has been spoken by the Tathāgata for the benefit of those beings who have set out upon the supreme vehicle, and for the benefit of those who have set out upon the most excellent vehicle,
from that moment, O Blessed One, knowledge has arisen within me.
"Blessed One, never before have I heard such a Dharma discourse as this.
Blessed One, those bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this sutra being spoken, will produce the perception of reality, will be endowed with the highest wonder."
For what reason? Because,
O Blessed One, whatever this perception of reality is, that itself is a perception of unreality.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says, "The perception of reality is the perception of reality."
"It is not surprising to me, Blessed One, that I should understand and have faith in this Dharma-discourse as it is being spoken.
But those beings, Blessed One, who will exist in the future time, in the final age, in the final period, during the last five hundred years when the true Dharma is in decline—
those who will take up, preserve, recite, and master this Dharma-discourse, [it is they who are truly marvelous]."
And they will reveal it in detail to others;
they will be endowed with the utmost wonder.
Furthermore, Blessed One, the notion of a self will not arise in them.
The notion of a sentient being will not arise, nor the notion of a living soul, nor the notion of a person; nor will any notion at all, nor even non-notion, arise for them.
Why is that?
O Blessed One, that which is the notion of a self is itself a non-notion;
that which is the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a living soul, or the notion of a person— [is likewise a non-notion].
That itself is non-perception.
For what reason?
Because the Buddha Bhagavats have indeed transcended all perceptions.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Those beings, Subhūti, who shall not be terrified when this sūtra is being spoken here will be endowed with the most supreme wonder."
They will be terrified, yet they will not fall into terror.
Why is that?
Subhūti, this which has been taught by the Tathāgata as the supreme perfection is, in fact, a non-perfection.

And that which the Tathāgata, Subhūti, calls the supreme perfection, that same [perfection] all the immeasurable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, also proclaim; therefore it is called the "supreme perfection."
Moreover, Subhūti, that perfection of patience of the Tathāgata is itself a non-perfection.
For what reason?
Subhūti, when King Kali cut away the flesh from my limbs and members,

at that time I had no perception of a self, nor a perception of a sentient being, nor a perception of a life-force, nor a perception of a person; indeed, I had neither any perception nor any non-perception.
For what reason?
If, Subhūti, at that time I had possessed the notion of a self, then at that time I would also have possessed the notion of malice.
If there had been the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a living soul, or the notion of a person, then at that time I would also have had the notion of malice.
Why is that?
Subhūti, I recall that in the past, during five hundred lifetimes, I was a seer who preached patience;
even then, I had no perception of a self, nor did I have a perception of a sentient being.
There was no perception of a living being (*jīva*),
nor any perception of a person (*pudgala*).
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having abandoned all perceptions, should resolve their mind upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should not generate a mind that is established in form;
one should not generate a mind that is established in sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena; one should not generate a mind that is established in any phenomenon whatsoever.
One should not give rise to a mind established in non-dharma,
nor should one give rise to a mind established anywhere.
Why is that?
That which is established is itself unestablished.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says: "A bodhisattva should give a gift without being established;
one should not give a gift while being established in form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena."
Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should indeed perform such an act of relinquishing gifts for the sake of all sentient beings.
Why is that?
Because this which is called the "notion of a sentient being," Subhūti—
That itself is non-perception. Those who are spoken of by the Tathāgata as all sentient beings are themselves non-sentient beings.
For what reason?
Subhūti, the Tathāgata is a speaker of what has become;
the Tathāgata is a speaker of truth, a speaker of reality, a speaker of that which is not otherwise,
and the Tathāgata is not a speaker of falsehood.
Moreover, Subhūti, as for that dharma which has been fully awakened to, taught, and contemplated by the Tathāgata— in that there is neither truth nor falsehood.
It is just as if, Subhūti, a man who has entered into darkness could see nothing at all.
In this way, a bodhisattva who gives away a gift while fallen into objective entities is to be viewed as such.
Subhūti, just as a man with sight might see various kinds of forms when the night has turned to dawn and the sun has risen,
so too is a bodhisattva who gives away a gift without falling into objective entities to be viewed.
Moreover, Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up this Dharma-discourse, bear it in mind, recite it, master it,
and reveal it in detail to others—
Subhūti, they are known by the Tathāgata through his Buddha-knowledge.
Subhūti, those beings have been seen by the Tathāgata with his Buddha-eye;
they have been known by the Tathāgata.
Subhūti, all those beings will produce and receive an immeasurable and incalculable mass of merit. 14.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a woman or a man were to sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges during the morning time, and likewise sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges during the midday time, and sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges during the evening time;
In this manner, one might sacrifice many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodily existences;
yet, whoever, having heard this Dharma discourse, does not reject it, would on that account produce a far greater mass of merit— immeasurable and incalculable.
How much more so for one who, having written it down, should take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and reveal it in detail to others?
Moreover, Subhūti, this Dharma discourse is indeed inconceivable and incomparable.

And this Dharma discourse, Subhūti, has been taught by the Tathāgata for the benefit of those beings who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle, for the benefit of those beings who have set out upon the Preeminent Vehicle.
Subhūti, those who shall take up this Dharma-discourse, retain it, recite it, master it,
and reveal it in detail to others,
will be known by the Tathāgata through his Buddha-knowledge.
Subhūti, those beings have been seen by the Tathāgata with his Buddha-eye; they have been known by the Tathāgata. Subhūti, all those beings will be endowed with an immeasurable mass of merit.
They will be endowed with a mass of merit that is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and infinite.
Subhūti, all those beings will, by their equal share, uphold, recite, and master awakening.
Why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, it is not possible for beings of inferior inclination to hear this Dharma-discourse;
nor for those with a view of a self, a view of a being, a view of a soul, or a view of a person.
It is not possible for beings who have not made the vow of a bodhisattva to hear, or take up, or bear in mind, or recite, or master this Dharma-discourse.
This possibility does not exist.
Moreover, Subhūti, whatever spot of earth this sutra shall be proclaimed, that spot of earth will become worthy of worship by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras;
that spot of earth will become worthy of salutation and worthy of circumambulation.
That spot of earth shall become like a shrine (caitya). // 15 //

Moreover, Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to such sūtras as these, and shall reveal them in detail to others—
They will be despised, and they will be thoroughly despised.
For what reason?
Moreover, Subhūti, whatever unwholesome karmas those beings have committed in previous lives that would lead to rebirth in the lower realms,
they will exhaust those unwholesome karmas of previous lives through being treated with contempt in this very life,
and they shall attain the awakening of a Buddha.

I recall, Subhūti, that in the past, more than incalculable, even more than incalculable eons ago, beyond even Dīpaṃkara the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, there were eighty-four hundred thousand million billion Buddhas whom I pleased; having pleased them, I did not displease them.

And, Subhūti, as for those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, whom I have pleased and having pleased, whom I have not displeased; and as for those who, in the future time, in the final period, during the last five hundred years when the true Dharma is being destroyed, will take up and uphold such sūtras as these— [they shall do so].
They will recite it, master it,
and reveal it in detail to others;
moreover, Subhūti, compared to this mass of merit, that former mass of merit does not approach even a hundredth part.

It does not bear comparison even to a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-quadrillionth part;
it does not admit of any calculation, fraction, reckoning, analogy, resemblance, or even the slightest point of comparison.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if I were to describe the mass of merit of those sons of good family or daughters of good family— indeed,
the mass of merit that those sons of good family or daughters of good family will produce and receive at that time— [it would be immeasurable].
Sentient beings might fall into insanity or undergo derangement of mind.
However, Subhūti, this Dharma discourse spoken by the Tathāgata is indeed inconceivable and incomparable; its maturation alone is to be expected as something inconceivable. 16.

Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should one who has set out on the bodhisattva vehicle abide; how should they practice; and how should they restrain the mind?"

The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, one who has set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle should generate the following thought: 'I must lead all sentient beings to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Even though he has thus led all sentient beings to final nirvana, not a single sentient being has been led to final nirvana.
Why is that?"
Subhūti, if the notion of a "sentient being" should arise in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a "bodhisattva";
or if the notion of a "living soul," up to the notion of a "person," should arise.
He should not be called a "bodhisattva.
For what reason?
Subhūti, there is no such dharma whatsoever that can be named "one who has set out on the bodhisattva vehicle."

(Vajr, Vaidya 84) "What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any dharma whatsoever which was fully awakened to as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the Tathāgata in the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, there is no such dharma, Blessed One, which was fully awakened to as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the Tathāgata in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One Dīpaṃkara."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is.

There is no dharma whatsoever, Subhūti, which has been fully awakened to as unexcelled perfect enlightenment by the Tathāgata from the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
If, however, Subhūti, there were any dharma that had been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata..."
The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied of me: "Young man, in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni.

But because, Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that has been fully awakened to as unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, therefore I was prophesied by the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara: "Young man, in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni."
For what reason?
Subhūti, "Tathāgata" is a designation for suchness (*bhūtatathatā*). Subhūti, "Tathāgata" is a designation for the nature of non-arising (*anutpādadharmatā*).
"O Subhūti, 'Tathāgata' is a designation for the cessation of phenomena.
O Subhūti, 'Tathāgata' is a designation for that which is absolutely unarisen. Why is that?"

Subhūti, this non-arising is that which is the ultimate truth. Subhūti, whoever should say, "The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment," would be speaking falsely.
Subhūti, he would be misrepresenting me by grasping at what is non-existent.
Why is that?
Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And, Subhūti, that dharma which has been fully awakened to or taught by the Tathāgata—in it there is neither truth nor falsehood.
Therefore the Tathāgata says: "All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
For what reason?
"Subhūti, 'all dharmas' are spoken of by the Tathāgata as non-dharmas;
therefore they are called 'Buddha-dharmas.'"
"Subhūti, it is just as if there were a man who possessed a body, a great body.
The Venerable Subhūti said: "Blessed One, that man whom the Tathāgata has described as possessing a body, a great body—that, Blessed One, has been described by the Tathāgata as being no-body."
Therefore, it is said that he is "endowed with a body" and "possessing a great body."
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Subhūti.
Any bodhisattva who should say, 'I shall bring sentient beings to final nirvāṇa,' should not be called a bodhisattva."
For what reason?
Is there, Subhūti, any dharma whatsoever that is called a "bodhisattva"?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
"There is no such dharma as one called a 'bodhisattva'.
The Blessed One said: "O Subhūti, 'beings, beings'—these have been spoken of by the Tathāgata as non-beings;
therefore they are called 'beings'."
Therefore the Tathāgata says: "All phenomena are selfless; all phenomena are devoid of a living being, devoid of a nourisher, and devoid of a person."
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall bring about the array of the buddha-field," he would speak falsely.
Why is that?
"Arrayed fields, arrayed fields," Subhūti—those have been described by the Tathāgata as non-arrays.
Therefore they are called "arrayed fields."

Subhūti, that bodhisattva who is convinced that "dharmas are selfless, dharmas are selfless" has been designated as a "bodhisattva mahāsattva" by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. // 17 //
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, Blessed One;
the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, Blessed One; the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, Blessed One;
the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, Blessed One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, Blessed One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? As many as there are grains of sand in the great river Ganges, have those grains of sand been spoken of by the Tathāgata?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, Blessed One."
"So it is, Sugata;
the sands have been spoken of by the Tathāgata.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? As many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the great river..."
There might be just as many rivers Ganges, or as many grains of sand in them, or as many world-systems as that.
"Would those world-systems be many?
Subhūti said, "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata."
"Those world-systems would be many.
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, as many sentient beings as there are in those world-systems, I know their various streams of thought."
For what reason?
Subhūti, "the stream of mind, the stream of mind"—this has been described by the Tathāgata as a non-stream;
therefore it is called "the stream of mind."
For what reason?
Subhūti, the past mind is not apprehended;
the future mind is not apprehended.
The present mind is not apprehended. // 18 //

What do you think, Subhūti? If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to fill this trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm, with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, would [that person] on that account [generate much merit]?
"Would that son of good family or daughter of good family, on that account, produce a great mass of merit?
Subhūti replied, "A great deal, Blessed One; a great deal, Sugata."
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
That son of good family or daughter of good family would produce from that cause a great mass of merit, immeasurable and incalculable.
Why is that?"
"A mass of merit, a mass of merit," Subhūti, that has been described by the Tathāgata as "not a mass.
Therefore it is called "a mass of merit.
If, moreover, Subhūti, there were such a thing as a mass of merit, [the Tathāgata would not have spoken thus].
The Tathāgata would not have spoken of "a mass of merit, a mass of merit. // 19 //
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Tathāgata to be perceived by means of the perfection of the form-body?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Tathāgata is not to be perceived by means of the perfection of the form-body."
For what reason?
"The perfection of the form-body, the perfection of the form-body," O Blessed One—this has been spoken of by the Tathāgata as non-perfection.
Therefore it is called "the perfection of the form-body."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, is a Tathāgata to be perceived by means of the perfection of physical marks?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One;
a Tathāgata is not to be perceived by means of the perfection of physical marks."
For what reason? Blessed One, that perfection of marks which has been spoken of by the Tathāgata has been spoken of by the Tathāgata as the absence of perfection of marks.
Therefore, it is called the "perfection of the marks. // 20 //
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Does it occur to the Tathāgata thus: 'Dharma has been taught by me'?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One; it does not occur to the Tathāgata thus: 'Dharma has been taught by me'.
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, whoever should say: 'Dharma has been taught by the Tathāgata'..."
He would speak falsely;
he would misrepresent me, Subhūti, by grasping at what is non-existent.
Why is that?
"Teaching of the Dharma, teaching of the Dharma," Subhūti—there is no such dharma whatsoever that can be apprehended by the name "teaching of the Dharma."
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Will there be, Blessed One, any beings in the future time,
in the final period, in the final age, during the last five hundred years when the true Dharma is being destroyed,
who, having heard such teachings as these, will have faith in them?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, they are neither beings nor non-beings.
Why is that?
Subhūti, all those who are called 'beings,' Subhūti, have been described by the Tathāgata as non-beings."
Therefore they are called "sentient beings. // 21 //
"What do you think, Subhūti— is there any dharma whatsoever which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Venerable Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
“Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said, “So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Not even the slightest dharma exists there, nor is it apprehended.”
Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. // 22 //
Furthermore, Subhūti, that dharma is equal; therein there is nothing unequal.
Therefore it is called "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
By way of selflessness, being-ness-less, lifeless, and personless, this unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is equal; it is fully awakened to by means of all wholesome dharmas.
For what reason?
Subhūti, as for "wholesome dharmas, wholesome dharmas," they have been described by the Tathāgata as indeed non-dharmas;
therefore they are called "wholesome dharmas. // 23 //

Furthermore, Subhūti, if some woman or man were to collect as many heaps of the seven precious jewels as there are Sumerus, kings of mountains, in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system, and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;

and if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to take up from this Dharma-discourse of the Perfection of Wisdom even a single four-line verse and teach it to others— [the latter would generate much more merit].
Subhūti, compared to this mass of merit, that former mass of merit does not approach even a hundredth part; indeed, it does not even bear comparison. // 24 //
What do you think, Subhūti? Does it occur to the Tathāgata that "I have liberated sentient beings"?
Indeed, Subhūti, it should not be viewed in this way.
Why is that?
Subhūti, there is no sentient being whatsoever who has been liberated by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any sentient being who had been liberated by the Tathāgata,
that itself would constitute the Tathāgata’s grasping at a self.
"Subhūti, if there were a grasping at a being, a grasping at a soul, or a grasping at a person,
it would be a grasping at a self; yet this which has been taught by the Tathāgata as 'grasping at a self' is actually a non-grasping, though it is apprehended by foolish common people."
"Subhūti, those called 'foolish common people' have been described by the Tathāgata as being no people at all;
therefore they are called 'foolish common people.'"
"What do you think, Subhūti—should the Tathāgata be viewed by way of the perfection of his physical marks?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said,"
"A Tathāgata is not to be seen by means of the perfection of physical marks.
The Blessed One said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just so, Subhūti."
It is just as you say.
A Tathāgata is not to be seen by means of the perfection of physical marks.
Why is that?
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a Tathāgata were to be seen by way of the perfection of physical marks,
then even a universal monarch would be a Tathāgata.
Therefore, a Tathāgata is not to be seen by way of the perfection of physical marks.
The Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, a Tathāgata is not to be seen by way of the perfection of physical marks."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Those who saw me by my form, and those who followed me by my voice—those people, being intent on false exertions, shall not see me. // 1 //

The Buddha is to be seen through the Dharma, for the Guides are the Dharma-body; yet the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not an object of cognition, and it cannot be fully comprehended. // 2.26 //
"What do you think, Subhūti? Was supreme, perfect enlightenment realized by the Tathāgata through the possession of the marks?
Indeed, Subhūti, you should not view it in that way.
And why is that?"
For it is not, Subhūti, by means of the perfection of physical marks that the Tathāgata has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, no one at all should say: "By those who have set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle, the destruction or annihilation of any dharma has been taught.
Moreover, Subhūti, you should certainly not view it in such a way.
For what reason? Because for those who have set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle, no phenomenon has been designated as subject to destruction, nor as subject to annihilation. // 27 //

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
and if a Bodhisattva were to attain the patient acceptance of the selflessness and non-arising of all phenomena— [the latter would generate far more merit].
On that account, this very person would generate a much greater mass of merit—immeasurable and incalculable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not grasp at a mass of merit.
The Venerable Subhūti said: "But, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva not grasp at a mass of merit?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is to be embraced, but not to be grasped.
Therefore it is called 'to be embraced.'"
Furthermore, Subhūti, if anyone were to say, "The Tathāgata goes or comes, stands or sits, or lies down," Subhūti, he does not speak of me.
He understands the meaning of what has been spoken.
Why is that?
Subhūti, it is said that the Tathāgata has not gone anywhere, nor has he come from anywhere.
Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. // 29 //

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to reduce to such ink all the particles of earth in a trichiliocosm— the number of world-systems being as great as those particles— and were to do so with such incalculable effort that it would be, for example, like a heap of atoms: what do you think, Subhūti, would that heap of atoms be great?
Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
That accumulation of atoms would be vast."
For what reason?
If, Blessed One, that accumulation of atoms were a substantial entity,
the Blessed One would not have called it "an accumulation of atoms."
For what reason?
O Blessed One, that which was spoken of by the Tathāgata as a "collection of atoms" was spoken of by the Tathāgata as "not a collection."
Therefore it is called a "collection of atoms.
And that which the Tathāgata has called the "trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm world-system," that was called a "non-system" by the Tathāgata.
Therefore it is called a "trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm.
For what reason?
If, Blessed One, there were such a thing as a world-system, [it would not be called a world-system].
That very grasping at a whole would not have occurred; and that which was called "grasping at a whole" by the Tathāgata—

"That which has been spoken of by the Tathāgata as 'grasping at a whole' is not grasping; therefore it is called 'grasping at a whole. The Blessed One said: 'Furthermore, Subhūti, this grasping at a whole is beyond conventional usage and is inexpressible.'"
It is neither dharma nor adharma;
yet it has been grasped by foolish common people. // 30 //
For what reason? Subhūti, if anyone were to say this: "The view of a self was taught by the Tathāgata;
the view of a sentient being, the view of a living soul, and the view of a person were taught by the Tathāgata," [they would speak falsely].
"Would he, Subhūti, speaking correctly, be speaking thus?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One; certainly not, Sugata."
One speaking correctly would not say so.
Why is that?
Blessed One, that which was called "the view of self" by the Tathāgata—
That which is called "view of self" has been described by the Tathāgata as "no-view"; therefore it is called the "view of self."
The Blessed One said: "In this way, Subhūti, one who has set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle should know, see, and resolve upon all phenomena.
And they should be known, seen, and resolved upon in such a way that one does not stand even in the notion of 'phenomenon,' nor in the notion of 'non-phenomenon.'"
For what reason?
Subhūti, that which is called "the notion of phenomena" is preached by the Tathāgata as being non-notion; therefore it is called "the notion of phenomena. // 31 //

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to fill immeasurable and incalculable world-systems with the seven precious jewels and offer them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;

and if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take up from this Dharma-discourse of the perfection of wisdom even a single four-line verse, and would memorize, teach, recite, and master it— [the latter would generate a far greater merit].
And if one were to reveal it in detail to others,
this alone would, on that account, produce a much greater mass of merit— immeasurable and incalculable.
And how should one reveal it?
Just as a star in the sky, an optical illusion, a lamp, a magical trick, a dewdrop, a bubble, a dream, a flash of lightning, and a cloud— so should the conditioned be viewed.
One should illuminate it in such a manner;
therefore, it is said that "one should fully illuminate it."

Thus spoke the Blessed One, and with joyful minds, the elder Subhūti, those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as those bodhisattvas and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Noble Vajracchedikā, the Blessed Perfection of Wisdom, is completed.
